title: The History of Monster Hunter | From PS2 To Wilds | Gaming History
description: The history of Monster Hunter: the 2004 PS2 original, the PSP boom in Japan, Monster Hunter World in 2018, Rise in 2021 and Wilds in 2025, with Capcom's 100 million sales milestone.

sections.heading: The hunt begins
sections.script: Welcome back to the channel. Today we are going through the history of Monster Hunter, Capcom's huge action series about hunting giant creatures. The idea is simple. You pick a weapon, travel to a wild area, learn how a monster behaves, defeat it, and use its parts to craft better gear. Then you do it again with an even bigger monster. This loop has pulled in tens of millions of players around the world. But it did not become a global hit overnight. In fact, the series spent many years as a Japanese phenomenon before the rest of the world noticed. In this video, we will follow the whole journey, from the first game on PlayStation two to the newest releases.

sections.heading: The original in 2004
sections.script: The first Monster Hunter launched in Japan on March eleventh, two thousand four, for the PlayStation two. Kaname Fujioka is credited as its creator. It was a different kind of game for its time. There were no experience levels. Your power came from your weapons and armor, and from your own skill and knowledge. Fights could be slow and demanding, and teamwork online made them more exciting. The game built a loyal fan base with its unique focus on crafting and preparation. Capcom saw the potential, and the studio started planning a long-term series. It was a quiet start compared to what came later, but all the core ideas were already there.

sections.heading: PSP and the Japanese boom
sections.script: The series really exploded in Japan on a handheld. Monster Hunter Freedom launched on the PlayStation Portable in Japan on December first, two thousand five, and Monster Hunter Freedom two followed on February twenty second, two thousand seven. Ryozo Tsujimoto has been the producer of the series since Freedom two, according to Wikipedia. Friends could sit together and hunt as a team using local connections, which made the games a social event. Monster Hunter Portable three rd, released in Japan in two thousand ten, was described by one writer as the best selling PSP game of all time. Players met in cafes and trains to hunt together, and the series became a real cultural trend in Japan.

sections.heading: Tri and the Wii era
sections.script: In two thousand nine, Monster Hunter Tri arrived on the Nintendo Wii, bringing the series to a home console with online play and underwater hunting. It was an important step because it showed that Capcom wanted the game to be played on both handheld and home devices. The series also continued on the Nintendo three D S with games like Monster Hunter four Ultimate and Generations, which kept the Japanese audience happy. While the West was still a smaller market, fans there grew steadily. Many players discovered the series through these entries and learned to love its weapon types, such as the Great Sword, the Long Sword, the Bow and the Hunting Horn. That fan base was ready for the next big step.

sections.heading: Monster Hunter World
sections.script: On January twenty sixth, twenty eighteen, Monster Hunter World launched worldwide at the same time, which was a first for the series. It was built for PlayStation four, Xbox One and later PC, with a seamless open ecosystem, a scoutflies tracking system and easier online play. It became the best selling game in the series and the best selling game in Capcom's history. Capcom reported it had passed twenty five million copies, and the company noted that it had sold more than one million units every year since release. For many players around the world this was the first Monster Hunter they ever played, and it changed how the series was seen outside Japan.

sections.heading: Rise on Nintendo Switch
sections.script: Monster Hunter Rise launched on the Nintendo Switch on March twenty sixth, twenty twenty one. It focused on speed, with the Wirebug that let hunters swing and dash through the map, and the Palamute, a dog companion you could ride. It also introduced the Rampage mode, a tower defense style event. The game was later released on other platforms, and in May twenty twenty four Capcom reported that it had reached fifteen million units. Together with World, it brought the series to a new level of popularity. Rise showed that Monster Hunter could work well on a portable system without losing its depth, and it brought many Switch players into the series.

sections.heading: The movie
sections.script: In December twenty twenty, a live action Monster Hunter film was released. It was directed by Paul W. S. Anderson, who also made the Resident Evil film series. The movie brought a story about soldiers who enter a world full of giant monsters, and it introduced the series to some viewers who had never played the games. Opinions on the film were mixed, but it showed how much the brand had grown. The series also appeared in other media, including merchandise, concerts and events. Monster Hunter had moved from a niche Japanese hit to something with global recognition, and Capcom was clearly ready to invest in it as one of its biggest pillars.

sections.heading: One hundred million
sections.script: In May twenty twenty four, Capcom announced that the worldwide cumulative sales of the Monster Hunter series had passed one hundred million units. It was the first Capcom series to reach that milestone, and it came about twenty years after the first game. World and Rise together accounted for nearly half of that total, which shows how much the recent entries changed the picture. Capcom also noted that older games kept selling. The milestone told a clear story. A series that started as a slow, demanding experiment on PlayStation two had grown into a global giant by staying true to its core idea, which is learning a monster and mastering your tools.

sections.heading: Monster Hunter Wilds
sections.script: Monster Hunter Wilds launched worldwide on February twenty eighth, twenty twenty five, on all platforms at the same time. Reports said it sold over eight million units in its first three days, and later Capcom results showed more than ten million copies by the end of its fiscal year on March thirty first. The game features large open regions that change with the weather and the seasons, and monsters that interact with each other in the environment. It continued the series' tradition of bigger fights, better visuals and more connected worlds. Wilds shows how far the series has come since the days when the whole team gathered around handheld screens in Japan.

sections.heading: Weapons, crafting and community
sections.script: What makes the core loop so special is how the pieces fit together. Each of the weapon types plays almost like a different game, from the quick Dual Blades to the heavy Hammer. Each monster drops parts that become armor and weapons, so every victory leads straight to the next challenge. The community also matters. Players share tips, build guides and help newcomers learn their first hunts, much like the groups that gathered with their handhelds in Japan in the PSP days. That sense of learning together is one of the best parts of the series, and it explains why people return to the same monsters again and again.

sections.heading: Why the hunt continues
sections.script: So why has Monster Hunter lasted so long? Because every fight teaches something. You learn a monster's moves, craft armor from its parts, and return stronger. Playing with friends makes it even better, and every new game adds new weapons, new monsters and new ideas. Now it is your turn. Which Monster Hunter game was your first, and which monster gave you the most trouble? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe to the channel for more gaming history videos. Thank you for watching, and happy hunting. We will see you in the next one.

joke: In Monster Hunter you spend twenty minutes fighting a dragon, then three hours farming its tail.
